title: Freud and Lacan
keyWorks: S. Freud, The Interpretation of Dreams (1900)
S. Freud, Civilization and Its Discontents (1930)
J. Lacan, “The Mirror Stage as Formative of the Function of the I” (1949)
J. Lacan, Seminar VII: The Ethics of Psychoanalysis (1959–1960)
J. Lacan, Seminar XI: The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis (1964)
summary: Psychoanalysis, created by Sigmund Freud and rethought by Jacques Lacan, starts from the idea that much of our mental life is unconscious — that is, it operates without our knowing. Lacan added that the unconscious is “structured like a language,” and that the human being is a desiring creature whose desire is born of lack.
onEmotions: For psychoanalysis, feelings are not malfunctions but messages: through them speaks what we don’t yet know about ourselves. Freud showed that an affect can “move” from one thought to another, so the cause of a feeling is not always where it seems to be. Lacan insisted that desire is always bound up with the Other — with language, culture, the people whose recognition we seek. The task is not to get rid of a feeling but to find words for it. Here we explain ideas rather than give clinical advice: psychoanalysis is, above all, a conversation.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is agonizing, and there is nothing shameful in it. Freud first saw it as a “dammed-up” drive, and later as a signal: the psyche’s way of warning itself that something it can’t yet cope with is approaching. Lacan went further. In his seminar Anxiety he argues that anxiety, contrary to popular belief, is “not without an object”: it arises when we come too close to the desire of the Other — to the question “What do they want from me?” — and don’t know the answer. That is why Lacan considered anxiety the affect you can trust more than the others: it points to something genuine, even if we can’t name it. From this point of view, anxiety doesn’t have to be silenced straight away: you can listen to it as a messenger who has come on real business.
anxiety.practice: Finish the sentence: “It seems to me that right now I’m expected to…” — and see whose expectation it is: yours or someone else’s.

quote.text: Anxiety is that which does not deceive.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan

fear.text: Fear is a natural reaction, and it often protects you. Freud distinguished fear from anxiety: fear has a definite object — a dog, an exam, a difficult conversation — while anxiety is diffuse and nameless. Curiously, psychoanalysis sometimes sees fear as a kind of relief. In the famous case of “Little Hans,” a boy was afraid of horses, and Freud showed that this fear gathered a vaguer anxiety around a single image and gave it shape. Lacan later said that such an object of fear serves as a support: it sets a boundary where otherwise there would be formless anxiety. You could put it this way: your fear probably has a direct meaning, but it may carry something else as well. Acknowledging fear doesn’t oblige you to conquer it at once — it’s enough to ask what it is saying besides the obvious.
fear.practice: Name your fear in one word, then ask yourself: “And if this weren’t there, what would I be afraid of then?” Just notice what comes to mind.

sadness.text: Sadness is a legitimate feeling; it needs no justification. Freud saw sorrow as the normal work of a psyche learning to let go of something dear. Lacan said something unexpected and uncomfortable about sadness: in his address Television (1973) he called it “moral cowardice.” He meant not a reproach to the person but a retreat from the duty of “speaking well” (bien dire) — finding the precise words for one’s desire. Sadness, for Lacan, often appears where desire has fallen silent, where we have stopped asking what we really want. This sounds stern, but there is hope in it too: sadness is not a verdict but a sign that some desire is waiting to be named. You don’t have to drive sadness away; you can let it lead you to that unspoken word.
sadness.practice: Write one sentence beginning with “What I would really like is…”, and don’t correct it.

grief.text: Grief is not an illness or a weakness but a natural response to loss. In “Mourning and Melancholia” (1917), Freud described the “work of mourning”: the psyche returns again and again to every memory, every hope connected with what was lost, and gradually, piece by piece, lets them go. It is slow and painful, and that is how it should be — there’s no need to rush the process. Lacan added that loss tears “a hole in the real” — in the very fabric of life — and a person fills it with symbols: words, rituals, farewells. That is why funerals, anniversaries, stories about someone who is no longer here matter so much: they help express loss when it seems there are no words. Grief, from this point of view, is the labor of love, not its end.
grief.practice: Recall one concrete detail connected with what you have lost — a gesture, a smell, a phrase — and write it down. This too is part of the work of mourning.

loneliness.text: Loneliness can be very hard, and there’s nothing strange about feeling it. Freud wrote that a human being begins life in a state of complete helplessness (Hilflosigkeit) and so needs another from the very start. Lacan added a sober thought, expressed in his famous and often misunderstood formula “there is no sexual relationship.” He meant that two people never add up to a whole without remainder: their desires never fully coincide. You can hear this as sad news, or as freeing news: your loneliness doesn’t prove that something is wrong with you. Everyone has a certain separateness, even in the closest relationships. And it is precisely thanks to this gap between people that speech, desire and encounter are possible.
loneliness.practice: Notice who or what exactly you are missing right now, and write down one sentence you would like to hear at this moment.

anger.text: Anger is a living, legitimate feeling: it tells you that something matters to you. In “Aggressivity in Psychoanalysis” (1948), Lacan linked aggression to the “mirror stage”: we build our ego by recognizing ourselves in an image — in a mirror or in another person. So the other both resembles us and seems to occupy our place, and this gives rise to rivalry. Anger often flares up precisely in this “imaginary,” mirror-like field: “they’re just like me, but they pulled it off.” Lacan, recalling the poet Charles Péguy, also described anger as the feeling that arises when the little pegs won’t go into the holes meant for them — when reality doesn’t fit the expected order. Seen this way, anger doesn’t make you a bad person; it shows where something didn’t match.
anger.practice: Finish: “It makes me angry that it was supposed to be like this, and it turned out like that…” — and see which expectation parted ways with reality.

shame.text: Shame is a very painful and very human feeling; everyone knows it. For Lacan, shame is closely tied to the gaze. In The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis he describes the gaze as one of the forms of the “object a” — his name for what causes our desire and anxiety yet can never be fully grasped. Shame is the moment when you suddenly find yourself seen, as if caught in the act, and cannot control how you are seen. Lacan takes up Sartre’s example: a man peeping through a keyhole suddenly hears footsteps behind him. Importantly, this gaze is often more imagined than real: we feel ashamed before an Other we carry inside ourselves. Understanding this doesn’t cancel shame, but it loosens its grip a little.
shame.practice: Ask yourself: “Whose gaze am I imagining right now?” — and try to describe this imaginary onlooker. Do they match anyone real?

guilt.text: Guilt can weigh very heavily, and that doesn’t mean you are a bad person. In Civilization and Its Discontents (1930), Freud described a strange paradox of the “superego” — the inner agency that watches and judges: the more a person submits to its demands and renounces their desires, the stricter it becomes. That is why guilt is often strongest in the most conscientious people. In The Ethics of Psychoanalysis, Lacan turned the question around: the only thing one can truly be guilty of is giving ground on one’s desire — betraying what really matters to you. This is not a call to do whatever you like, but a question of being true to yourself. From this point of view, it helps to distinguish real responsibility for a specific act from an endless inner tribunal that always demands more.
guilt.practice: Divide a sheet into two columns: “what I’m really responsible for” and “what the inner voice accuses me of.” Look at how they differ.

envy.text: Envy is unpleasant and people tend to hide it, but everyone knows it. Lacan loved an example from Augustine’s Confessions: an infant, pale with envy, watches his foster brother at the breast. Lacan notes that the little one is already fed himself — he envies not the milk but the picture of another’s fullness, an image in which the other seems whole and satisfied. That is envy in general: we rarely want the thing itself; we want the happiness we imagine it gives the other. Hence Lacan’s famous idea that our desire is born through the Other. Once you see this, envy becomes a clue rather than a verdict: it shows what image of fullness attracts you — and reminds you that the person you envy has a lack of their own.
envy.practice: Consider what exactly you see in the person you envy: what feeling or state do you attribute to them? Write it down in one word.

quote.text: Man’s desire is the desire of the Other.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan
quote.source: Seminar XI: The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis (1964)

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can be very heavy — this is not laziness or whim. In “Mourning and Melancholia,” Freud noticed an important difference: in mourning it is the world that seems impoverished, while in melancholia it is the ego itself that feels poor and empty. He explained it this way: when a loss is not recognized, “the shadow of the object falls upon the ego,” and a person seems to lose a part of themselves. Lacan offered another view: emptiness is not always an enemy. In The Ethics of Psychoanalysis he uses the image of the potter who creates a vase around emptiness: without the void there is no vessel. Lack, for Lacan, is the place from which desire is born. Perhaps your emptiness is not an absence of life but a space where a new desire has not yet found its name. If it lasts a long time, it’s worth talking about it with someone you trust.
emptiness.practice: Ask yourself: “If one small desire could appear in this emptiness, what would it be?” Even “I don’t know” is an answer.

quote.text: In mourning it is the world which has become poor and empty; in melancholia it is the ego itself.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud

confusion.text: Confusion is a normal state when familiar landmarks stop working. Freud called the discovery of the unconscious the third blow to human self-love — after Copernicus and Darwin: it turned out that our conscious ego does not run the whole of our mental life. Lacan wrote the subject as a barred letter, $: we are divided, not fully transparent to ourselves, and part of what drives us speaks through slips of the tongue, dreams, recurring situations. From this point of view, confusion is not a malfunction but an honest moment when you touch that division. It doesn’t need to be hastily closed with a ready-made answer. Psychoanalysis values exactly such moments: something you didn’t know about yourself may sound in them.
confusion.practice: Write down three thoughts that are spinning in your head right now, without trying to reconcile them. Is there one among them that surprised you?

quote.text: The ego is not master in its own house.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud
quote.source: “A Difficulty in the Path of Psycho-Analysis” (1917)

fatigue.text: Fatigue and burnout are real exhaustion, not a weakness of character. Freud described the “superego” as an inner overseer whose demands can never be fully met. Lacan added an unexpected twist: the superego demands not only “you mustn’t” but also “enjoy!” — be happy, productive, successful. He called the superego an imperative of jouissance — a word that means not simple pleasure but a strained “too much” that verges on pain. Lacan also distinguished demand — which can be satisfied — from desire, which is never sated. Burnout can be understood as an attempt to answer the Other’s endless demand completely, as if it could be closed. Admitting that this is impossible is not defeat but relief.
fatigue.practice: Write down whose voice in you says, “Just a bit more, you have to get it done.” What would you answer if you were talking to it out loud?

boredom.text: Boredom seems trivial, but it can be very oppressive — and it is an honest feeling. Neither Freud nor Lacan left a separate theory of boredom, but from a psychoanalytic perspective you could put it like this. Lacan believed that desire rests on lack and on the “object a” — the cause of desire, the elusive spark that makes anything attract us at all. Boredom is perhaps the state in which the objects around us are there but the spark is not: everything is available, yet nothing calls. This doesn’t mean desire has vanished — it simply hasn’t yet found where to go. Sometimes boredom is a useful pause: when the world stops offering ready-made answers, you get a chance to notice your own interest, not an imposed one.
boredom.practice: Remember the last time you were truly interested. What exactly drew you then — the thing itself, or something in it?

joy.text: Joy is a beautiful feeling, and it needs no justification. Psychoanalysis treats it attentively but without naivety. Freud described the “pleasure principle”: the psyche strives to reduce tension and reach equilibrium. Lacan distinguished from pleasure jouissance — “enjoyment,” an excessive, intense experience that can border on pain. From this point of view, joy is closer to pleasure: it is gentle and doesn’t demand “more and more.” Freud valued humor too: in his essay “Humour” (1927) he wrote that in a joke the strict superego suddenly comforts the frightened ego like a friend. Joy doesn’t have to be complete or eternal to be real. You can let it be small and simply stay in it.
joy.practice: Notice three bodily signs of your joy right now — in your breathing, your shoulders, your face — and give yourself a few seconds just to feel them.

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the deepest human experiences. Lacan spoke of love paradoxically: in it we give not things or virtues but our own lack — the admission that we are missing something and that the other matters to us. To love, for Lacan, is to open up, not to present yourself as flawless. Freud, for his part, noted that in love we often repeat early attachments and see in the beloved reflections of figures from the past. This doesn’t devalue the feeling — it simply shows that it is connected to your whole history. Psychoanalysis takes love seriously: the analytic conversation itself, for Freud, rests on “transference,” that is, on love. Your tenderness, from this point of view, is not weakness but the courage to reveal your lack.
love.practice: Consider: what do you really give to the one you love — not in things, but of yourself? Write down one word.

quote.text: Love is giving what you don’t have.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling. Psychoanalysis has written less about it than about anxiety or guilt, but there is an important exception. Melanie Klein, a psychoanalyst of the generation after Freud, showed in Envy and Gratitude (1957) that these feelings are two poles: envy spoils the good we receive, while gratitude lets us accept it and keep it inside. Lacan has another thought: every demand is, at bottom, a demand for love, and a gift is precious not for the object itself but for what it means: “you matter to me.” That is why gratitude often responds not to the thing but to the sign of attention. Allowing yourself to be grateful means admitting that you need others, and there is nothing humiliating in that.
gratitude.practice: Recall one recent sign of attention you received. What did it tell you, beyond the thing or the act itself?

hope.text: Hope is an important feeling; it helps you keep living. Psychoanalysis treats it with both respect and sobriety. In The Future of an Illusion (1927), Freud called an illusion a belief in which wish-fulfilment plays the leading part; it isn’t necessarily an error, but it’s useful to see what exactly we want. At the same time, Freud himself was a man of cautious hope: he believed in the slow but persistent power of reason and understanding. Lacan described desire as a movement that slides from one object to another and never comes to a final rest. Hope, from this point of view, is desire turned toward the future. It doesn’t need to know how everything will end; it’s enough that desire is alive and keeps searching.
hope.practice: Finish: “I hope that…”, and then: “And behind that lies a desire for…”. See what emerges in the second line.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia can be sweet and sad at the same time, and there is nothing childish about it. In Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905), Freud noted that every new attachment partly seeks something very early and long lost: we don’t so much find as recognize. Lacan developed this idea: the lost object, in a sense, was never in our hands in the fullness with which we remember it. Nostalgia longs not so much for the past as it was, but for the image of fullness that the past holds for us. This doesn’t devalue your memories — they are real. But you might notice that longing for “back then” says a lot about your desire “now.”
nostalgia.practice: Choose one memory you miss and ask: what feeling from it would I like to find in my life today?

quote.text: The finding of an object is in fact a refinding of it.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud
quote.source: Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905)

craving.text: A sharp craving — “I want it right now” — can be very strong, and there is nothing shameful in it. Lacan distinguished three things: need (hunger, thirst), demand (a request addressed to another) and desire — what remains beyond them and is never fully satisfied. A craving promises: “This is it, and then everything will be fine.” But having got the thing, we often feel the familiar Lacanian “that’s not it.” From this point of view, a cigarette, a drink or a phone takes the place of something else — something hard to name. This doesn’t make you weak; this is how desire works for everyone. What helps is not so much prohibition as a question: what exactly am I hoping to get in this second — calm, closeness, oblivion?
craving.practice: When a craving comes, finish the sentence: “If I got it right now, I would feel…” Look at the last word: that is what you are really looking for.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure but a circle that is genuinely hard to get out of. In Civilization and Its Discontents, Freud wrote about this without judgment: life is too hard for us, and people seek “palliative measures” — distractions, substitutes, intoxicating substances. He acknowledged that the last of these act quickly, but soberly noted the cost: they drain energy that could go into changing one’s life. In Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920), Freud described the “repetition compulsion” — the psyche’s tendency to return to what brings no pleasure. Lacan linked this to jouissance — something beyond simple pleasure that holds us even when it causes pain. Psychoanalysis suggests not shaming yourself but starting to speak: what has been named loses some of its power.
addiction.practice: Write: “This helps me not to feel…” If you’d like, think about whom you could talk to about it — someone close, a professional, or a mutual-help group.

quote.text: Life, as we find it, is too hard for us; it brings us too many pains, disappointments and impossible tasks. In order to bear it we cannot dispense with palliative measures.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud

hangover.text: The morning after is hard: your body aches, and on top of that come anxiety, shame and gaps in memory. It’s an understandable state, and it doesn’t make you a bad person. In Group Psychology, Freud wrote about festivals: in them familiar prohibitions are lifted for a while, and a person feels free. But then the “superego” returns — the inner agency that judges, forbids and punishes. From this point of view, a “moral hangover” is the return of a strict inner judge who sometimes punishes far more harshly than what happened deserves. Lacan would add: the anxiety about “what did I do last night” is a question about the gaze of the Other. It helps to distinguish what really happened from what the judge inside fills in.
hangover.practice: Divide a sheet into two parts: “what I know for sure” and “what I’m imagining.” Fill in both and see which is longer.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a strong, joyful experience: everything seems possible. There’s no need to be suspicious of it right away. In Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego, Freud observed that a feeling of triumph arises when something in us coincides with our “ego ideal” — the image of who we would like to be. For a moment the distance between “who I am” and “who I want to be” vanishes, and everything feels light and bright. From this point of view, euphoria is not a deception but a precious moment of coinciding with yourself. Psychoanalysis only adds that such coincidence is by nature temporary, because desire lives on distance. That is no reason to cloud the high, but a reason to enjoy it without demanding that it last forever.
euphoria.practice: Ask yourself: “Which image of myself am I matching right now?” Write down how you feel yourself to be right now — it’s a valuable clue to your ideals.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high can be hard: the world fades, and it seems it will always be like this. It’s an understandable reaction. Freud described how, after a festival or a moment of triumph, the ego and the ego ideal part ways again: the distance between who we are and who we want to be reappears, and it feels like a loss. Lacan would add that this is how desire is built: what we’ve achieved often loses its shine, and we feel the familiar “that’s not it.” From this point of view, the comedown is neither proof that the joy was fake nor the truth about your life. It is the return of lack, from which, for Lacan, desire is born. The slump will pass, and lack will once again become what moves you.
crash.practice: Write: “Right now I’m missing…” — and don’t rush to fill it in. Just acknowledge that lack is part of being alive.

panic.text: A panic attack is genuinely frightening: your heart, your breathing, the feeling “I’m about to die or go mad.” Such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Freud was one of the first to describe such attacks in detail, and he distinguished two kinds of anxiety. “Signal” anxiety warns of danger. “Automatic” anxiety floods us when the psyche can’t process tension in time — Freud saw its prototype in the helplessness of infancy. Lacan would say that in such moments we collide with the “Real” — what cannot be put into words. From this point of view, two things help: support for the body now, and words later. Once the wave has passed, telling the story of it already begins to make it less formless.
panic.practice: Put your feet flat on the floor and feel them. Make your exhale longer than your inhale and name aloud five objects around you. Later, if you want, describe what you went through in words.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what is all this for,” the sense of the abyss and of finitude — is familiar to many, and there is nothing abnormal about it. In the essay “Thoughts for the Times on War and Death” (1915), Freud observed that it is impossible truly to imagine our own death: in the unconscious each of us is, as it were, convinced of our own immortality. That is why the thought of finitude intrudes as something alien and frightening. Lacan called the “Real” whatever doesn’t fit into language and images — and dread arises when we come too close to it. From this point of view, the answer is not to find a final explanation but to keep speaking: language, bonds with people, desire — these are what human beings build at the edge of the abyss, and that building is life itself.
dread.practice: Write down three things you want — not things you “should,” but things you actually want. Desire, for Lacan, is what keeps us in life.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone is living more interesting lives while you are “in the wrong place” is very common and very painful. Lacan would explain it like this: our desire is always bound up with the Other. We want not simply things but what others find desirable, what seems recognized. Social media is the perfect machine for this kind of desire: it shows not people’s lives but their shop window, someone’s “imaginary” image — Lacan’s name for the register of pictures and mirror reflections. From this point of view, the fear of missing out is less about events than about the question: “Where is the thing I actually want?” You won’t find the answer in someone else’s feed. Lacan considered the central ethical question to be “Have you acted in conformity with the desire that is in you?” — in you, specifically.
fomo.practice: Recall what triggered your fear of missing out. Ask yourself: “Do I want this, or do I want to be seen there?” Write down the honest answer.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and three-in-the-morning thoughts are exhausting. At night there are no tasks to distract you, and the psyche starts to speak louder. Freud called the dream the “guardian of sleep”: it turns anxious thoughts into images so that we can keep sleeping. When there is too much anxiety, this guardian can’t cope, and we wake up or can’t fall asleep. From this point of view, night thoughts are not the truth about your life but material the psyche didn’t manage to process during the day. Lacan would stress that the unconscious speaks in language: a recurring night thought is like a sentence that hasn’t yet been heard to the end. You don’t need to resolve it at night. It’s enough to write it down and set it aside for a conversation — with yourself or with someone — during the day.
sleepless.practice: Write down the night thought in one sentence, exactly as it sounds. In the morning, reread it: which words in it seem most important?

quote.text: Dreams are the guardians of sleep and not its disturbers.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: what collapses is not only trust in a person but your picture of the world. This pain is legitimate. Lacan distinguished two levels of relationship. The “imaginary” is the level of images: we see in the other who we would like them to be. The “symbolic” is the level of the word, of promises, of agreement, on which trust rests. Betrayal is a breaking of one’s word, and that is why it hurts so much: it strikes at what life among people itself depends on. Lacan also said that the Other is always “incomplete”: no person can be a total guarantee. From this point of view, betrayal doesn’t prove you were foolish. It painfully reveals what no one wants to know: there are no guarantees, and yet people go on giving their word.
betrayal.practice: Write one sentence: “I believed that he/she…” Look at it: is this about the real person, or about an image you loved?

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonizing, and almost everyone knows it. In a 1922 paper on jealousy, Freud called its “normal” form one of those affects better not denied: he believed that someone who seems not to feel it at all is more likely repressing it. He distinguished jealousy based on a real threat from “projected” jealousy, in which we attribute our own unconscious desires to the other. Lacan loved an example from Augustine’s Confessions: an infant, pale with jealousy, watches his brother at the breast. For Lacan this is a scene of the “imaginary”: the other seems to possess what we lack. From this point of view, jealousy often speaks not only of your partner but also of your own lack — and that can be explored without shame.
jealousy.practice: Finish the sentence: “It seems to me the rival has something I don’t have — namely…” See what it is really about.

resentment.text: An old grievance is heavy: you carry it around, and it flares up again and again. Almost always there is a real injustice behind it. In “Remembering, Repeating and Working-Through” (1914), Freud noted that what we cannot remember and fully put into words, we tend to repeat. Lacan would add an uncomfortable but freeing thought: in the way we cling to a grievance there is a hidden jouissance of its own — the bitter satisfaction of being right, a bond with the one who hurt us that won’t let us release them. This doesn’t mean “it’s your own fault”: this is how the psyche works for everyone. From this point of view, a grievance needs not prohibition but working-through — finally being spoken in full.
resentment.practice: Ask yourself honestly: “What does this grievance give me? What would I lose if it weakened?” Write down whatever comes to mind.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains, and it needs time. Freud described this state with rare precision. In “Mourning and Melancholia,” he speaks of the “work of mourning”: slowly, one memory at a time, the psyche withdraws its attachment from a person who is no longer there. It is agonizing precisely because it happens gradually, and each memory has to be lived through again. Lacan would add that in love we give our lack, and so a breakup exposes it especially sharply. From this point of view, your pain is not weakness but work that is taking its course. It can’t be hurried by command, but you can avoid getting in its way: let yourself remember, talk, cry.
heartbreak.practice: Choose one memory of the person and tell it — on paper or out loud. That is a small step in the work of mourning.

quote.text: We are never so defenceless against suffering as when we love, never so helplessly unhappy as when we have lost our loved object or its love.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud

impostor.text: The fear that you’re about to be “found out” is agonizing and familiar to a great many people, especially conscientious ones. Freud described the paradox of “those wrecked by success”: sometimes a person struggles not with failure but precisely with the fulfilment of a wish, as if they had no right to it. Lacan went further. In his view, every role we have — “doctor,” “manager,” “specialist” — is given to us from outside, from the symbolic order, rather than growing out of our nature. So everyone who is honest with themselves feels a gap between themselves and their title. Lacan said that a king who seriously believes he is a king is no less mad than a madman. From this point of view, your gap is not exposure but a sign of sobriety.
impostor.practice: Write down your role, and next to it three things you actually do in it. The role may be “borrowed clothes,” but the work is yours.

quote.text: If a man who thinks he is a king is mad, a king who thinks he is a king is no less so.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan

self_hatred.text: When an inner voice keeps saying that you are worthless, it hurts terribly. That voice is wrong, even if it sounds convincing. Freud called this agency the “superego” and noticed its strangeness: the stricter a person is with themselves, the harsher it becomes — obedience never satisfies it. In “Mourning and Melancholia,” he suggested that cruel self-reproaches are often really addressed to someone else — an important person one wasn’t allowed to be angry with — and have been turned inward. From this point of view, the inner critic is not the voice of truth about you but someone else’s voice, absorbed long ago. Psychoanalysis doesn’t suggest arguing with it, but asking: whose words are these? Once you recognize them, it’s easier to stop taking them for your own.
self_hatred.practice: Write down your inner critic’s most frequent phrase and ask: “Who once spoke to me like this, or something like it?”

helplessness.text: Helplessness is a heavy and ancient feeling. Freud believed that human life begins with it: for a long time an infant cannot help itself, and this original helplessness (Hilflosigkeit) makes us creatures who need others. That is why, for Freud, in moments of adult powerlessness a very early, almost childlike fear returns so easily. From this point of view, your feeling is not evidence of weakness but the echo of a deep experience shared by all people. There’s something else too: out of infant helplessness grew not only anxiety but also speech and connection with others. The answer to helplessness has essentially always been to reach out — a request, a story, a call. That is still a possible step now.
helplessness.practice: Write down what you would ask for right now if you could ask anyone at all. Consider whom you could tell at least part of it.

procrastination.text: “I can’t get started” is not laziness, and psychoanalysis looks at it with curiosity rather than reproach. In Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety, Freud described “inhibition”: the psyche restricts some activity so as not to run into anxiety. Sometimes starting is frightening because a beginning brings closer an evaluation, a possible failure — or, on the contrary, success and the expectations that come with it. Lacan noted that desire is often sustained by what remains unfulfilled: as long as the task hasn’t been started, it can be as perfect as you like. From this point of view, procrastination is a message, not a defect: something about the task is making you anxious. What helps is not pressure but a question: what will change if I begin?
procrastination.practice: Finish the sentence: “If I start this, I’ll have to face…” Then take the smallest possible first step — just open the file.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — after a move or emigration — can be very hard: you lose your ground, your language, familiar faces, the whole life you were used to. It is a real loss, and it deserves to be mourned. Freud knew it from the inside: in 1938, already gravely ill, he was forced to emigrate from Vienna to London. Lacan emphasized that the human being exists in language: our “native” language is not a tool but the fabric our “I” is made of. That’s why living in a foreign language can sometimes feel like living slightly outside your own skin. In his essay “The Uncanny,” Freud noted that the German word unheimlich (uncanny) comes from Heim — home. From this point of view, your longing is grief that needs time and words, in any language.
uprooted.practice: Say aloud or write down a phrase in your native language that you haven’t spoken in a long time — a saying, a line, a word used only at home. Notice what it brings up.

overload.text: Overload and the endless feed wear you out: it seems there’s no free space left inside. In Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920), Freud described a “protective shield against stimuli”: the psyche is shielded from too strong a flow of impressions, and when this shield is breached, an overload arises that it can’t keep up with. Lacan would add something unexpected: our superego can not only forbid but also command “Enjoy!” — watch more, learn more, don’t miss out. From this point of view, endless scrolling is not weakness of will but a response to that command. You can allow yourself what this voice can’t stand: to stop, to not know everything, to leave something unread.
overload.practice: Put your phone down and tell yourself: “I give myself permission not to find out anything for the next ten minutes.” Notice what happens in your body.

unreality.text: The feeling that everything around you, or you yourself, isn’t quite real can be strange and frightening. It deserves gentle care. Freud described such an episode from his own life. In the open letter “A Disturbance of Memory on the Acropolis” (1936), he recalls how, standing on the Acropolis, he felt a strange estrangement: as if what he was seeing wasn’t entirely real. Freud didn’t decide he was “broken”; he set out to explore what the feeling meant, and linked it to deep experiences from his past. From a psychoanalytic point of view, a feeling of unreality is also a message: sometimes this is how the psyche holds at a distance what is too much to feel directly right now. You don’t have to fight it; you can calmly lean on sensations and words.
unreality.practice: Describe aloud what you see, as if telling a friend: “In front of me there’s a table, and on it a cup…” Words help restore your connection to the world.

quote.text: So all this really does exist, just as we learnt at school!
quote.author: Sigmund Freud
quote.source: A Disturbance of Memory on the Acropolis (1936)

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience. In Civilization and Its Discontents, Freud discussed with the writer Romain Rolland the “oceanic feeling” — a sense of connection with something limitless. Freud honestly admitted that he himself hardly knew it, but he took it seriously and suggested that it recalls a very early state, when the “I” had not yet separated from the world. Lacan described “sublimation” as raising an object “to the dignity of the Thing” — when something ordinary suddenly glows with something greater than itself. From this point of view, awe is a moment when the boundary between you and the world grows thin for a second. It doesn’t need to be fully explained; you can simply treasure it.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with whatever filled you with awe. Try to describe it in a single sentence — and notice what words can’t convey.

relief.text: Relief is a pleasant feeling: something has let go, and you can breathe out. Allow yourself to have it without reservations. Freud believed that the psyche is largely governed by the “pleasure principle” — the drive to reduce painful tension. Relief is the experience of that reduction in its pure form. Back in Studies on Hysteria, Freud and Breuer noticed that when a painful experience can be put into words, liberation follows — they called this “catharsis.” And in his book on jokes, Freud wrote that laughter arises when energy we had been spending on holding back is released. From this point of view, relief shows how much strength was going into the tension. You can take note of exactly what eased it.
relief.practice: Write one sentence: “I felt better when…” It’s a clue to what helps you.

calm.text: Calm and peace are precious states that need no justification. Oddly enough, psychoanalysis knows a lot about calm, because it knows a lot about unrest. For Lacan, the human being is a desiring creature, and desire never falls completely silent. So calm is not the absence of desire but a moment when it doesn’t press or demand to get something urgently. Freud recommended a special state to analysts — “evenly suspended attention”: listening without grasping at anything and without pushing anything away. From this point of view, your calm is like that kind of attention to your own life: anything can be, and nothing is needed right now. You can simply be in this state.
calm.practice: For a minute, listen to the sounds around you, without singling any out or pushing any away. Just let them be.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a vivid, living state in which you want to create. Freud used the word “sublimation” for the process by which powerful drives find a new path — into art, science, work — and saw it as one of civilization’s highest achievements. Lacan rethought sublimation as the capacity to raise an ordinary object “to the dignity of the Thing”: a word, a sound, a line suddenly begins to carry something greater than itself. From this point of view, inspiration is the moment when your desire finds a form. Lacan believed it matters not to give ground on your desire. So it’s good to give inspiration an outlet straight away, while the desire is hot — without judging, comparing, or asking whether anyone needs it.
inspiration.practice: Spend ten minutes letting your inspiration take shape: a sketch, a note, a couple of lines. Don’t edit.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude — pleasure at someone else’s failure — is usually embarrassing to admit even to yourself. But psychoanalysis begins precisely by not turning away from such feelings. Lacan described the “mirror stage”: our ego is formed from an image, and next to it there is always a double — another who resembles us, with whom we compete for place and recognition. He called this dimension the “imaginary.” When a rival stumbles, for a moment it seems there is more room for us. In his book on jokes (1905), Freud noted that many jokes give an outlet to aggression we usually hold back. From this point of view, schadenfreude is not proof of your malice but a trace of this old struggle for a place. You can notice it and ask: who am I comparing myself with right now?
schadenfreude.practice: Finish: “If he/she lost, then I…” The answer will show you what rivalry lives in you and what you really want.

contempt.text: Contempt seems cold and confident, but something more vulnerable often hides behind it. In Civilization and Its Discontents (1930), Freud described the “narcissism of minor differences”: people push away most strongly from precisely those who resemble them — neighbors, relatives, closely related groups. A small difference is needed to emphasize one’s own separateness. And in “On the Universal Tendency to Debasement in the Sphere of Love” (1912), he showed how the psyche can divide people into the exalted and the “low” in order to cope with an inner conflict. From this point of view, contempt often pushes away in another what too closely resembles ourselves, or what we don’t want to see in ourselves. This doesn’t make you a bad person. It makes contempt interesting: you can question it.
contempt.practice: Write down what exactly you despise in this person. Then ask yourself: has this trait ever — even a little — been in me, or in what I’m afraid of?

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong bodily feeling, sometimes directed at others, sometimes at a situation, sometimes at yourself. It doesn’t make you bad. In Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905), Freud described disgust, shame and morality as “dams” — mental forces built up in the course of development to restrain and channel the drives. He also noted that intense disgust is sometimes a “reaction formation”: the psyche turns attraction into repulsion so as not to encounter a desire. This doesn’t mean that a desire hides behind every disgust — often it simply protects. But from a psychoanalytic point of view, disgust is worth not only enduring but also listening to: it speaks of a boundary that matters to you, and sometimes of something that has come too close to that boundary.
disgust.practice: Ask yourself: what is disgust protecting me from right now? Write down the first thought that comes, without judging it.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge usually grows out of a real hurt: you were caused pain, and justice demands a response. This feeling is understandable. Freud did not consider people naturally peaceful: in Civilization and Its Discontents he wrote about a deep-rooted inclination to aggression that civilization is forced to restrain somehow. But psychoanalysis draws a strict line between thought and deed. Fantasies of revenge can be stormy — they are psychic reality, not a crime. The danger lies in “acting them out,” bypassing words. Freud put the aim of analysis this way: where an impersonal drive operates, an “I” should appear that can become aware of it and choose. From this point of view, revenge can be given a place in words — in writing, in conversation — and then it stops giving the orders.
revenge.practice: Write a letter to the person who hurt you that you will never send — with all your anger, uncensored. Then note what you would want most: punishment, acknowledgment, or an apology.

quote.text: Where id was, there ego shall be.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud
quote.source: New Introductory Lectures on Psycho-Analysis (1933), Lecture 31

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to you — a partner, parents, children — can burn, and shame follows. Here psychoanalysis is rather reassuring. Melanie Klein showed that the mixing of love and anger begins very early: an infant experiences its mother now as “good,” now as “bad,” and only gradually understands that she is one and the same person. Klein called this step the “depressive position” — not an illness but a stage of growing up, in which we learn to bear that the one we love and the one we are angry with are the same person. From this comes the wish for “reparation” — to make amends, to take care, to restore the bond. From this point of view, anger does not cancel love. What matters is neither to pour it out on the person you love nor to hide it from yourself, but to give it words — and then to come back with care.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger has calmed, ask yourself: “What do I want to restore in our relationship?” Sometimes reparation is a single warm sentence.

ambivalence.text: To love and be unable to stand the same person at the same time is agonizing, but it is one of the most common human experiences. The word “ambivalence” itself was introduced by the psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler, and Freud made it one of his key concepts: in Totem and Taboo (1913) he showed that toward the most important people — parents, lovers, teachers — our feelings are almost inevitably double. Lacan even coined the word hainamoration — “hateloving,” a fusion of hatred and being in love. From this point of view, mixed feelings don’t mean that something in the relationship is irreparably broken or that you “don’t know how to love.” Rather, they mean this person truly matters to you. You don’t have to resolve the ambivalence immediately; you can let both sides speak.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a sheet into two columns: “What I love in you…” and “What I can’t stand in you…”. Fill in both without crossing anything out, and see how they sit side by side.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, after a loved one’s death, or after their long, grave illness often brings shame with it: how can I feel lighter? But relief and love can live side by side. In Totem and Taboo (1913), Freud noted that after the death of a loved one people often torment themselves with reproaches. He explained this by saying that in any deep attachment, besides tenderness, there is also weariness and hidden resentment, which we are ashamed of and don’t acknowledge. From a psychoanalytic point of view, relief is partly the voice of that unacknowledged weariness. And it doesn’t cancel love or mean you are a bad person. It may mean that a long strain has ended — and it can give you the strength to grieve for real.
guilty_relief.practice: Write: “I feel lighter because what has ended is…” — and separately: “I miss…”. Let both sentences be true.

indifference.text: Sometimes, where something “ought” to move you — someone else’s misfortune, important news, even a loss — there is silence inside. It’s frightening, but indifference rarely means you truly don’t care. Freud described a mechanism he called “isolation”: the psyche separates an idea from the affect attached to it, so that an event can be known without being felt at full strength. He also noted that affect can “relocate” — appearing later, over some other, seemingly trivial occasion. From this point of view, numbness is not coldness of character but a form of defense, often temporary: the psyche is protecting you until it is ready to take in what happened. There’s no need to force yourself to feel “the right way.” You can simply note: my feelings are on pause right now — and let them come in their own time.
indifference.practice: Notice whether in the past few days you’ve had an unexpectedly strong reaction to something small — tears at a film, irritation over a trifle. Sometimes feeling arrives exactly like that, by a detour.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything and leave — your job, your city, your familiar role — is familiar to a great many people. It isn’t foolish: often it is the voice of weariness with a life that has become too cramped. Lacan described desire as “metonymy”: it slides from one object to another, because it is really aimed not at a particular thing but at a lack that no thing ever fully closes. Freud showed that fantasies are not empty daydreams but scenes in which we fulfil our wishes. From this point of view, it is worth listening seriously to your escape fantasy: who do you become there, whose gaze are you freed from, what do you finally allow yourself? Often “drop everything” means “stop living up to other people’s expectations.” You can understand this without making any big decisions yet.
escape.practice: Describe your escape fantasy in detail: where you are, what you’re doing, who isn’t around. Then underline what you want most.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is “off limits” — an unavailable person, the “wrong” person — can be confusing and frightening. But in itself it says nothing about what you will do, and psychoanalysis approaches it without moralizing. In The Ethics of Psychoanalysis, Lacan drew attention to the words of the apostle Paul: “I would not have known sin except through the law.” From this he concluded that prohibition and desire are more tightly linked than they seem: what is “forbidden” itself becomes attractive. Moreover, for Lacan, desire is aimed not so much at a person as at the “object a” — the elusive cause of desire, which always slips away a little. From this point of view, it’s useful to ask not “Is this right?” but “What in me responds to this unavailability?”
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down what exactly attracts you: the person themselves, their unavailability, or who you become around them. Just observe, without drawing conclusions.

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment can make simple things — walking into a room, starting a conversation, making a call — very hard. It is a common and understandable experience. Lacan described how, at the “mirror stage,” a child recognizes itself in its reflection and turns to an adult for confirmation: “Is that me?” From then on, part of our ego rests on another’s gaze and approval. Lacan called the “big Other” the authority before which we seem to be constantly sitting an exam — language, rules, an imaginary judge. In shyness this judge becomes especially loud. But the real people in the room are usually far less preoccupied with us than the inner examiner is. From this point of view, you can gradually learn to tell living companions apart from the onlooker we carry inside.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, ask yourself: “Who am I really afraid of right now — these people, or my inner examiner?” Try to describe its voice.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is exhausting: you can’t plan, there’s nothing to lean on. The wish to know in advance is natural. Here psychoanalysis says something unexpected: no one has complete knowledge. Lacan described the analyst as the “subject supposed to know”: a person comes hoping that someone knows the answer, and gradually discovers that no such all-knowing Other exists. Lacan depicted this as the “barred” Other: language, society, authorities are incomplete too. At first this is frightening, but there is freedom in it as well: if no one knows for sure, then your not knowing is not a personal failure but a shared condition of life. Even Freud, in his late paper “Analysis Terminable and Interminable” (1937), admitted that the work of understanding itself is never finished. From this point of view, uncertainty can be carried as a shared burden.
uncertainty.practice: Write down the question that torments you, and beneath it: “Right now, nobody knows this.” Notice how the feeling changes.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, news — stretches time and stops you from living: everything seems to be on pause. Freud once watched his eighteen-month-old grandson playing with a wooden reel on a string: he would throw it over the edge of his cot with a long “o-o-o-o” (Freud understood it as fort — “gone”) and joyfully pull it back: da — “there.” He described this game in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920) and interpreted it this way: the child, waiting for his absent mother, was turning helpless waiting into an action of his own, one he could control. From this point of view, waiting is especially agonizing when we are completely passive. Finding in it even a small area where you act for yourself makes it more bearable.
waiting.practice: Choose one small task that depends only on you, and do it while there’s still no answer. Notice how your sense of time changes.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn’t do can return again and again. This feeling says that it mattered to you. Psychoanalysis offers two ways of looking at it. Freud wrote about “deferred action” (Nachträglichkeit): the meaning of past events can change later, when we learn and live through something new. The past can’t be remade, but it can be retold — and that too changes what it means for you. And in The Ethics of Psychoanalysis, Lacan gave a provocative formula: true guilt lies in giving ground on your own desire, in betraying it. From this point of view, regret sometimes points not to a mistake to be mourned endlessly, but to a desire that is still alive and can be heard now.
regret.practice: Finish: “I regret it because what I really wanted was…” Then ask yourself whether this desire has a place in your life today.

quote.text: The only thing one can be guilty of is having given ground relative to one’s desire.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan
quote.source: Seminar VII: The Ethics of Psychoanalysis (1959–1960)

longing.text: Longing for a particular person can be almost physical: you miss their voice, their look, their presence. It is the natural price of a real bond. In “Mourning and Melancholia” (1917), Freud described the “work of mourning”: slowly, memory by memory, the soul relives each thread connecting it to the one who is absent, and only in this way gradually frees its energy for life. It can’t be hurried by command. Lacan would add that the person we love was for us not only themselves but also a place where we felt desired and seen. So we long both for them and for the self we were beside them. From this point of view, longing is not weakness but work that a loving soul does. It can be lived through gently, a little at a time.
longing.practice: Recall one specific detail about this person — a gesture, a pet word — and write it down. Details like these are the very material of the work of mourning.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — for wars, injustice, grim news — can press so hard that it’s difficult to live an ordinary life. This feeling speaks of your capacity for compassion. In 1915, at the height of the First World War, Freud wrote “Thoughts for the Times on War and Death,” in which he confessed to the same disillusionment and bewilderment that many felt. And in 1932, in his open letter to Einstein, “Why War?”, he ended on a note of cautious hope: whatever fosters the growth of civilization and the ties between people works against destruction. From this point of view, your pain is not naivety but part of those ties. But the psyche can’t hold other people’s suffering without limit. Taking care of your strength is not indifference but the condition for going on feeling.
world_pain.practice: Name one concrete bond you can support today — a conversation, some help, taking part. And separately, one time of day without news.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts as though it weren’t a request that was refused, but you as a whole. This pain is natural. Freud wrote about “narcissism” not in the everyday sense of vanity but as the healthy self-love everyone needs. Rejection inflicts a “narcissistic wound”: it strikes at the self-image we build partly out of how others receive us. Lacan showed that our ego is formed from the very beginning out of reflections — out of what we see in the mirror and in other people’s eyes. So someone else’s “no” can feel like a crack in the ego itself. From this point of view, it’s important to remember: a reflection is not yet you. One person’s refusal speaks of a meeting of two desires that didn’t match, not of your worth.
rejection.practice: Write down what exactly in you, as it seems, was “rejected.” Then ask yourself: is this a fact, or a reflection you have just mistaken for yourself?

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can be very deep and very old: it seems that without the other person the ground will give way. That’s understandable — we are born completely dependent on others. In Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety (1926), Freud considered the loss of a loved person, and later the loss of their love, to be among a child’s earliest situations of danger. Melanie Klein described how a child gradually “takes in” a good image of the caring adult, and this inner support remains even when the real person leaves the room. From this point of view, your present fear may carry an echo of very old experience. And at the same time, you most likely already have inner supports — people, voices, memories that have stayed with you.
abandonment.practice: Recall someone — from childhood or now — with whom you felt safe. Imagine their voice and what they might say to you right now.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love wounds painfully: the feeling is there, but there is no answer. That doesn’t make it any less real. In “On Narcissism” (1914), Freud noted that being in love is often accompanied by “overvaluation” of the beloved: they are endowed with perfections that largely belong to our own ideal. Lacan went further: we love in the other “something more than them” — the mysterious “object a,” which causes desire but never coincides with the living person. That is why unrequited love wounds twice over: we lose not only hope in the person but also the ideal we invested in them. From this point of view, you can try to discern what exactly you loved in them — and which part of it is really yours and can stay with you.
unrequited.practice: Write down three qualities you love in this person. Then mark which of them you would like to find or develop in your own life.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: it feels as though your dignity has been taken from you, often in front of others. This feeling is natural and doesn’t speak of weakness. Freud distinguished the ego from the “ego ideal” — the image of who we would like to be. Humiliation strikes precisely at the gap between them: we are, as it were, forcibly shown to be far from our own ideal. Lacan would add that humiliation unfolds in the “imaginary” register — in a play of images where someone tries to come out on top by making another lower. But the image imposed on you is not the whole truth about you: the subject, for Lacan, is always more than any reflection. From this point of view, you can separate the pain, which is real, from the verdict, which you don’t have to accept.
humiliation.practice: Write down what was said or done, and separately what conclusion about yourself you drew from it. Ask: whose conclusion is this — mine, or that of the person who humiliated me?

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be exhausting: the mirror becomes an exam. It is a very common feeling. In his paper on the “mirror stage” (1949), Lacan described how an infant, still clumsy and uncoordinated, suddenly sees a unified image in the mirror — and joyfully takes it for itself. Ever since, according to Lacan, a tension lives in us between how the body feels from the inside and a picture that “ought” to be smooth and whole. Freud stressed that the ego is bodily from the very start. From this point of view, body shame is not your personal whim but a crack built into the very way we become ourselves. It can be softened by returning more often from the picture to the living sensation: the body is not only an image but also the one who feels.
body_shame.practice: Close your eyes and for a minute feel your body from the inside: the warmth of your hands, your weight, your breathing. This is the body the mirror doesn’t show.

quote.text: The ego is first and foremost a bodily ego; it is not merely a surface entity, but is itself the projection of a surface.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud

illness.text: When your body lets you down — pain, illness, weakness — it’s hard, and irritation, fear and sadness are natural here. In “On Narcissism” (1914), Freud observed that a person tormented by pain or illness involuntarily withdraws interest from the outside world and concentrates on themselves. He quoted the poet Wilhelm Busch on a man with toothache: his whole soul lives “in his molar’s narrow hole.” Freud didn’t condemn this — he saw in it a natural movement of the psyche gathering its forces where it hurts. From this point of view, if right now it’s hard to be interested in anything but your own condition, that is neither selfishness nor weakness. Interest in the world usually returns when things get a little easier; for now, you can simply be more attentive to yourself.
illness.practice: Say to yourself one sentence you would say to a sick friend — gentle, without demands. Write it down and reread it when things are hard.

pride.text: Pride in what you’ve done is a deserved feeling, and there’s no need to hide it. Freud spoke of “narcissism” not only as a problem: everyone needs healthy self-love, and an important part of it is the sense of having come closer to your “ego ideal,” the image of who you want to be. When that happens, self-regard rises, and that is good. Freud used the word “sublimation” for the capacity to channel the force of the drives into work, creativity, knowledge — and pride often accompanies precisely such fruits. Lacan would add: it matters whose recognition you are seeking. Pride is especially stable when you yourself see the value of what you’ve done, rather than only waiting for others’ applause. From this point of view, you can allow yourself to rejoice — and notice which of your own desires has come true.
pride.practice: Write: “I’m proud that…” — and then: “This matters to me because…”. The second line will show you your own desire.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness is a quiet feeling in which sorrow is mixed with tenderness toward the world. It doesn’t need fixing. It’s important to make a distinction right away: for Freud, “melancholia” is a clinical concept describing a severe condition, while gentle sadness is something quite different. Closer to it is Freud’s short essay “On Transience” (1916). He recalls a summer walk with a young poet who could not enjoy the beauty of nature knowing that it would fade. Freud objected: transience does not take value away from beauty; on the contrary, it adds to it. From this point of view, gentle sadness is a way of feeling the value of what passes. You can live through it unhurriedly, like quiet music, without turning it into anxiety about loss.
melancholy.practice: Choose something fleeting nearby — light in a window, a smell, a sound — and spend a minute with it, knowing it will pass.

quote.text: Transience value is scarcity value in time.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud
